newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia may split off RAO UES's distribution unit.
newsitem.headline: Russia may split off RAO UES's distribution unit.

text.p: The Russian government may split off national electricity company RAO UES's distribution unit from the rest of the firm, Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Wednesday.

"There is a proposal to reconstruct the company in such a way as to pay big attention to the federal market of wholesale electricity and to make it accessible to a wider circle of users...and at the same time to split off the distribution unit as a separate, single state enterprise," he told a news conference.

He said the proposal would introduce competition into the power supply and distribution system by allowing individual power plants, known in Russian as energos, to offer supplies to consumers on a competitive price basis.
But he said it would not be necessary to formally break up the entire RAO Yedinaya Energeticheskaya Sistema Rossii (UES) structure.
"I don't consider a break-up of their organisations as necessary," he said, referring to UES and natural gas monopoly RAO Gazprom GAZP.RTS.

"We could say that several generating companies will appear in RAO UES, but that in any case there will be one general company, let's call it a transmission company, where there will be transmitting capacities, capacities of a host of hydro-electric stations. This company could regulate this entire sector," he said.

"The thing is that in any case a single energy system exists, and has its advantages. We must take them into account. But on the other hand we must increase competition. We will strive to introduce this competition within the parameters of this structure," he said.
UES is a national power company which owns the national power grid.
It owns 29 power plants, holds stakes in all but two of Russia's 72 "energo" regional utilities and is one of Russia's biggest companies by market capitalisation.
The state will keep a 51 percent stake in UES until the end of 1988.
Foreigners own approximately 20 percent of the company.
A consortium headed by Natsionalny Rezervny Bank, closely linked to Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, bought most of an 8.5 percent in UES at a recent auction.
